question_text: Find the equation of the plane if the foot of the perpendicular from the origin to the plane is (1, 3, −5).

mark_split.label: Read the normal off the foot

steps.label: Read the normal off the foot
steps.margin_note: First mark. The foot of the perpendicular gives two things at once: it is a point ON the plane, and the line from the origin to it is a normal to the plane.
steps.memory_tip: The foot of the perpendicular gives BOTH a point on the plane and the normal's direction ratios.

steps.why: The perpendicular from a point to a plane meets it along the normal direction, so the segment OP and the plane's normal are the same line. Its direction ratios are just the coordinates of P, because O is the origin.
common_mistakes: Using (1, 3, −5) only as a point and looking for the normal elsewhere.
Thinking a second point is needed, when the foot on its own fixes the plane.

steps.label: Write and simplify the plane
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Use the point-and-normal form with P as the point and OP as the normal. The z coordinate is negative, so z − (−5) becomes z + 5.
steps.memory_tip: The constant term is −35, and 35 = 1² + 3² + 5² is the square of the distance from the origin.

steps.why: The constant term is −35, and 35 = 1² + 3² + (−5)² is the square of the distance OP. That is a quick way to see the constant is right without expanding twice.

Leaving the answer as x + 3y − 5z = 0, which is a parallel plane through the origin.
